title: What training do insurance claims staff need in Australia?
description: Claims handling has been a licensed financial service since January 1, 2022. What INFO 253 and the General Insurance Code expect of claims staff training.
shortAnswer: Since January 1, 2022, handling and settling insurance claims has been a financial service under the Corporations Act 2001, so insurers and the claims managers, loss adjusters and assessors acting for them need an Australian financial services license and must keep claims staff adequately trained and competent under section 912A(1)(f). The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) sets out its training expectations in INFO 253, and the General Insurance Code of Practice adds training and record keeping commitments.
keyTakeaways: Schedule 7 of the Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response) Act 2020 removed the exclusion for claims handling; the licensing obligations applied from January 1, 2022 after a transition period that ended on December 31, 2021.
ASIC expects a training and competency framework for employee claims staff covering eight named topics, tailored to new starters and decision makers, with annual reviews of staff competency.

Responsible managers for a claims handling authorization are generally expected to have three years of relevant claims experience in the past five years plus a relevant degree or diploma level qualification.
The General Insurance Code of Practice (in effect from October 5, 2021, updated October 2023) requires education and training about the Code and records kept for at least 7 years.
A strengthened General Insurance Code was submitted to ASIC on October 22, 2026 and had not replaced the current Code as at November 2026.
regulator: Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC); Code Governance Committee for the General Insurance Code of Practice
appliesTo: General and life insurers that handle and settle claims under their own AFS license
Claims managers, loss adjusters, loss assessors and insurance brokers that handle claims on behalf of an insurer
Claimant intermediaries that represent or assist insured people in pursuing a claim
Insurance fulfilment providers and other service suppliers overseen by the licensee
Responsible managers, team leaders and claims decision makers

sections.heading: Why is claims handling now a licensed financial service?

blocks.text: Claims handling became a financial service because the Australian Government removed its long standing exclusion in response to the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry. Schedule 7 of the [Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response) Act 2020](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2020A00135/asmade/text), titled "Claims handling and settling services", amended the Corporations Act 2001 and commenced on January 1, 2021.

ASIC's [Information Sheet 253 (INFO 253)](https://www.asic.gov.au/for-finance-professionals/afs-licensees/apply-for-an-afs-licence/licensing-for-certain-service-providers/claims-handling-and-settling-how-to-comply-with-your-afs-licence-obligations) explains that from January 1, 2022, a business in a prescribed category that provides claims handling and settling services must hold an AFS license with a claims handling authorization, or be authorized by someone who does. ASIC accepted license applications from January 1, 2021, and the obligations apply to any claim made on or after that date that was still open when the transition period ended on December 31, 2021.

Under section 766G, the service covers nine activities, including stating an opinion that could influence a decision about making or continuing a claim, assisting a person to make a claim, assessing whether the insurer is liable, deciding to accept or reject all or part of a claim, quantifying the insurer's liability, and offering to settle. That breadth matters for training scope: call center staff who take first notice of loss and external loss adjusters both perform licensed activities.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the law, ASIC guidance and the General Insurance Code of Practice as at November 2026. INFO 253 was last updated in June 2025. Check the primary sources before relying on any date or paragraph number.

sections.heading: What does ASIC expect claims staff training to cover?

blocks.text: ASIC expects licensees to build a training and competency framework for employee claims staff, and it lists the topics that framework should include. The legal anchor is section 912A(1)(f) of the Corporations Act, which requires a licensee to ensure its representatives are adequately trained and competent to provide the service. ASIC says it does not prescribe specific arrangements: licensees may train directly, use a competent external provider, or rely on a representative's previous training.
Table 7 of the [INFO 253 PDF](https://download.asic.gov.au/media/q2ybygwo/info253-published-16-june-2025.pdf) says ASIC expects employee representatives to receive training in:

items: the specific products relating to the claims they handle and settle
the legal obligations that apply when handling and settling claims
the difference between financial product advice and a claims handling and settling service
obligations under the relevant code of practice
the licensee's claims processes and procedures
internal and external dispute resolution processes
how to identify and serve consumers experiencing vulnerability and financial hardship

blocks.text: ASIC adds that training should be tailored to different employees' needs and responsibilities, naming new starters and staff with decision making authority as examples, and that it expects licensees to "conduct annual reviews, or take various regular steps that constitute review, of staff competency". For representatives who are not employees, the licensee must still be satisfied they are trained and competent, for example by due diligence before engagement and by checking education, accreditation, experience and reputation.

sections.heading: Do claims staff need RG 146 qualifications?

blocks.text: Usually not, because handling and settling a claim is a different financial service from giving financial product advice. INFO 253 notes that the training standards for advisers "do not apply to persons who only provide general advice, or personal advice on products such as general insurance or consumer credit insurance".

The boundary becomes a training topic in its own right. INFO 253 gives the example of a claims officer who recommends an insurance product the claimant does not already hold: that recommendation is financial product advice, and the person must be authorized for advice and comply with Parts 7.7 and 7.7A of the Corporations Act. Staff who handle claims on more complex products such as life insurance, and who also advise, may fall under the adviser standards described on the [RG 146 page](/regulations/asic-rg-146-training-requirements). Teaching staff where the line sits, with scenario based assessment, is more defensible than a general awareness module.

sections.heading: What competence must responsible managers show?

blocks.text: The people a licensee nominates as responsible managers must show knowledge and skills specific to claims handling, because section 912A(1)(e) requires the licensee to maintain organizational competence. For a claims handling authorization, INFO 253 says ASIC generally expects responsible managers to have at least three years of relevant experience handling and settling insurance claims over the past five years, plus either a university degree in business, law, commerce, finance or another relevant field, or a diploma level qualification from a relevant professional body.

Managers who do not meet that profile can be assessed under the alternative options in Regulatory Guide 105, covered on the [RG 105 organizational competence page](/regulations/asic-rg-105-organisational-competence). Responsible managers, controllers and officers must also be fit and proper persons under section 913B. INFO 253 separately expects licensees to manage staff numbers and skills, and to have processes to scale up claims resources for large events such as natural disasters, which in practice means surge training for redeployed or contract staff.

sections.heading: What training does the General Insurance Code of Practice require?

blocks.text: The [General Insurance Code of Practice](https://insurancecouncil.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/2023-COP_UPDATE_October_FINAL.pdf), published by the Insurance Council of Australia, commits subscribing insurers to train employees and distributors and to keep the records. Paragraph 7 states that the Code took effect on October 5, 2021, and the current text was updated in October 2023. ASIC describes code membership as voluntary but "a strong indicator" of commitment to handling claims efficiently, honestly and fairly.

items: **Paragraph 28:** employees and distributors must receive appropriate education and training to provide their services competently, to deal with customers professionally, and about the Code.
**Paragraph 29:** employees' education and training records will be kept for at least 7 years and made available to the Code Governance Committee on request; distributors must do the same.
**Paragraph 31:** concerns about an employee's or distributor's conduct are investigated and may be addressed by requiring further training or by disciplinary action.
**Paragraph 38:** service suppliers must be qualified by education, training or experience to provide the required service competently.

**Paragraph 96:** internal policies and training appropriate to employees' roles help them understand whether a customer may be vulnerable and engage with sensitivity, dignity, respect and compassion.
**Paragraph 102:** relevant training for employees likely to be involved in communications requiring an interpreter.
**Paragraph 109:** internal policies and training to help employees identify financial hardship and decide how to provide support.

blocks.text: The claims part of the Code sets the service standards that training must teach. For example, paragraph 70 commits insurers to update the customer on progress at least every 20 business days, and paragraph 77 requires a claim decision within 4 months of receiving the claim unless an exception applies. INFO 253 says code timeframes are "useful indicators" of appropriate standards even for licensees that do not subscribe.

sections.heading: How do claims handling obligations map to roles and evidence?

blocks.text: Each obligation lands on a different group of people, at a different frequency, and leaves a different trail of evidence. sections.heading: How are claims handling and the Code monitored and enforced?

blocks.text: ASIC enforces the licensing obligations, and the Code Governance Committee monitors and sanctions breaches of the Code. Under paragraph 173 of the Code, the committee may require an insurer to take rectification steps within a set timeframe, audit its compliance at its own cost, or publish corrective advertising. Paragraph 180 requires an annual compliance report to the committee, and paragraph 181 requires a significant breach to be reported within 10 business days.

Claims conduct also carries court risk. In 2026 the Federal Court ordered Hollard Insurance to pay a $2 million penalty for breaching the duty of utmost good faith under the Insurance Contracts Act 1984 over a claim that took more than three years to finalize. ASIC's [release on the decision](https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/news-centre/find-a-media-release/2026-releases/26-236mr-hollard-fined-2-million-for-serious-insurance-claim-delay) quotes the court's finding that the delays "cannot be explained simply as the product of staff busyness", a reminder that training records alone will not answer a systemic failure.

blocks.title: Code in transition
blocks.text: The Insurance Council of Australia states on its [Code of Practice page](https://insurancecouncil.com.au/cop/) that it submitted a strengthened General Insurance Code of Practice to ASIC on October 22, 2026. As at November 2026 the October 2023 version remains the operative Code. Expect paragraph numbers and training commitments to change once a new Code is finalized, and plan a review of the training map at that point.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures the claims handling obligations, the eight INFO 253 training topics and the Code paragraphs as a framework linked to each claims role, then attaches an assessment point to each link. When the strengthened Code is finalized, the affected roles and assessments can be identified from the framework rather than by rereading every module, and each person's record shows which Code version they were assessed against.

faqs.q: Do outsourced loss adjusters need to be trained by the insurer?
faqs.a: Not necessarily by the insurer, but the insurer remains responsible for their competence. INFO 253 says that for representatives who are not employees, the licensee should establish identity, run due diligence before engagement, check any required license or registration, and otherwise satisfy itself through education, accreditation, experience and reputation checks.

Neither the Corporations Act nor INFO 253 sets a fixed training interval. ASIC does expect annual reviews of staff competency, or regular steps that amount to review. Many licensees meet that with an annual competency check plus targeted refreshers when products, procedures or the Code change.

faqs.q: How long must claims training records be kept?
faqs.a: Insurers that subscribe to the General Insurance Code of Practice commit under paragraph 29 to keep employees' education and training records for at least 7 years and to provide them to the Code Governance Committee on request. They must also require their distributors to do the same.

faqs.q: Does the claims handling regime apply to superannuation insurance claims?
faqs.a: Yes, where the claim involves an insurance product regulated by ASIC. INFO 253 explains that claims handling services are treated as provided to the insured person and to third party beneficiaries, such as members insured under a group life policy through a superannuation fund.
